archetypes.name: Recognize a Polynomial Graph
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §5.3 — Graphs of Polynomial Functions
archetypes.coreConcept: Polynomial graphs are continuous and smooth; they have no breaks, holes, or sharp corners.
archetypes.mentalModel: Check whether the curve can be drawn without lifting a pencil and without a sharp turn; both are structural properties of polynomial graphs.
archetypes.governingRelation: A polynomial function is continuous for every real input; its graph has no breaks or corners.

cognitiveTraps.description: Accepting a graph with a sharp corner as a polynomial graph.
Accepting a graph with a discontinuity as a polynomial graph.

archetypes.name: Factor to Find Polynomial Zeros
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §5.3 — Graphs of Polynomial Functions
archetypes.coreConcept: Real zeros are the inputs that make the polynomial equal zero; factoring turns the zero-product property into candidate inputs.
archetypes.mentalModel: Factor the expression, set each factor to zero, and keep the factor equation connected to the original function.

cognitiveTraps.description: Dropping a zero introduced by a common variable factor before solving the remaining factors.
Factoring correctly but failing to set every factor equal to zero.
Reporting the constant inside a linear factor instead of solving for the zero with its opposite sign.
Counting a repeated zero once for each repeated factor when the task asks for distinct zeros.
cognitiveTraps.trapFormula: sum distinct zeros counts r with multiplicity m more than once

archetypes.figureNone: A graph would reveal the requested zeros directly, so it would give away the target of a factoring problem.

archetypes.name: Read Zero Multiplicity from a Graph
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §5.3 — Graphs of Polynomial Functions
archetypes.coreConcept: At a real zero, odd multiplicity makes a polynomial graph cross the axis, while even multiplicity makes it touch and turn back.
archetypes.mentalModel: Near each intercept, inspect whether the curve changes sides of the axis; crossing parity distinguishes odd from even multiplicity.
archetypes.governingRelation: (x-r)^m: odd m crosses at r; even m touches and turns at r

cognitiveTraps.description: Reading a touch-and-turn zero as an odd multiplicity because the graph reaches the axis.
Assuming every crossing zero has multiplicity one, even when the curve flattens as it crosses.
Reporting the polynomial's total degree instead of the exponent on the factor for the named zero.

archetypes.name: Predict Polynomial End Behavior
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §5.3 — Graphs of Polynomial Functions
archetypes.coreConcept: The leading term determines polynomial end behavior: degree parity controls whether the ends agree, and the leading coefficient controls their direction.
archetypes.mentalModel: For large inputs, lower-degree terms matter less than the leading term; read parity and sign before sketching either tail.
archetypes.governingRelation: For f(x)=a_n x^n+...: even n gives matching ends, odd n gives opposite ends; sign(a_n) sets the right-end direction.

cognitiveTraps.description: Using coefficient sign alone and ignoring whether the degree is even or odd.
Reversing the end direction for a negative leading coefficient.

archetypes.figureNone: The problem supplies only degree and leading coefficient; a plotted curve would encode the requested end behavior.

archetypes.name: Bound Turning Points by Degree
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §5.3 — Graphs of Polynomial Functions
archetypes.coreConcept: A degree-n polynomial can have at most n−1 turning points.
archetypes.mentalModel: A degree-n polynomial can have no more than n real zeros and its smooth graph cannot reverse direction more than n−1 times.

cognitiveTraps.description: Using the degree itself as the maximum number of turning points.
Subtracting two instead of one from the degree.
Adding one instead of subtracting one when converting degree to the maximum turning-point count.

archetypes.figureNone: This is a direct symbolic bound; a graph would add no useful information.

archetypes.name: Sketch a Polynomial from Features
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §5.3 — Graphs of Polynomial Functions
archetypes.coreConcept: Zeros, multiplicities, leading coefficient, and one additional point determine a least-degree factored polynomial and its broad graph behavior.
archetypes.mentalModel: Build one factor per zero with its multiplicity, then use a known nonzero point to set the vertical scale and verify the end behavior.
archetypes.governingRelation: f(x)=a∏(x−r_i)^{m_i}; one known point determines a when it is not a zero

cognitiveTraps.description: Using a zero once even when its stated multiplicity requires a repeated factor.
Assuming the leading scale factor is one without checking the supplied point.

archetypes.name: Use the Intermediate Value Theorem
archetypes.source: OpenStax Algebra and Trigonometry 2e §5.3 — Graphs of Polynomial Functions
archetypes.coreConcept: For a continuous polynomial, opposite signs at two inputs guarantee at least one zero strictly between those inputs.
archetypes.mentalModel: Continuity prevents the graph from moving between opposite sides of the axis without crossing it; the theorem guarantees existence, not an exact root or uniqueness.
archetypes.governingRelation: If f is continuous on [a,b] and f(a)f(b)<0, then some c∈(a,b) has f(c)=0.

cognitiveTraps.description: Claiming the sign change proves exactly one zero in the interval.
Treating equal endpoint signs as proof that no zero lies between them.

archetypes.figureNone: A graph would visually reveal the guaranteed crossing; the drill targets the theorem's sign and continuity conditions.
